1. Breaking Changes

Section titled “1. Breaking Changes”

1.1 Qwen Portal OAuth Removal (#52709)

Section titled “1.1 Qwen Portal OAuth Removal (#52709)”

Background: Qwen (Tongyi Qianwen) previously integrated with portal.qwen.ai via qwen-portal-auth OAuth — an early authentication method. Alibaba Cloud has since unified the Qwen API under the Model Studio platform, and the old OAuth flow is no longer maintained.

Use Case: Users running Qwen series models (qwen-turbo, qwen-plus, qwen-max, etc.) as OpenClaw inference backends.

Example: Previously, selecting Qwen during openclaw onboard would launch a browser-based OAuth authorization flow. Now it requires a direct Model Studio API Key input:

Notes:

  • ⚠️ Breaking — Existing Qwen users must reconfigure authentication after upgrading
  • You’ll need to obtain an API Key from dashscope.console.aliyun.com first
  • If any cluster instances use Qwen, prepare new keys before upgrading

Comparison with Similar Products:

ProductQwen SupportAuth Method
OpenClaw✅ Model Studio API KeyAPI Key
ZeroClaw✅ Via OpenRouter/direct configAPI Key
Nanobot✅ Native supportAPI Key
NanoClaw❌ No direct supportN/A
PicoClaw❌ NoneN/A
IronClaw✅ Via configAPI Key + encrypted storage

Trend: LLM providers standardizing on API Key authentication is the clear direction — OAuth flows are too heavyweight for CLI tools.

1.2 Doctor Auto-Migration Window Tightened

Section titled “1.2 Doctor Auto-Migration Window Tightened”

Background: openclaw doctor previously auto-fixed legacy config keys of any age. Now it only auto-migrates keys from within the last two months; older ones trigger an error instead.

Use Case: OpenClaw instances that haven’t been upgraded for a long time running openclaw doctor.

Example: If an instance hasn’t been upgraded for 3 months and its config contains old-format keys from late 2025, doctor will no longer silently fix them — it will report a validation error requiring manual intervention.

Notes:

  • ⚠️ Cluster instances may trigger this if they’ve been dormant for a while
  • Recommended: run openclaw doctor on the current version before upgrading to ensure config is up to date

Comparison: Most similar products are too new to have config migration issues. ZeroClaw has zeroclaw migrate openclaw but that’s a one-time import, not continuous migration.

Trend: A sound engineering decision — unlimited backward compatibility accumulates technical debt.

2. Providers & Models

Section titled “2. Providers & Models”

2.1 xAI / Grok: Responses API + x_search (#56048)

Section titled “2.1 xAI / Grok: Responses API + x_search (#56048)”

Background: xAI (Elon Musk’s AI company) launched their Responses API (similar to OpenAI’s Responses API), along with x_search — a tool that can search X/Twitter real-time data. Previously, OpenClaw used xAI’s older Chat Completions API.

Use Case:

  • Grok models now automatically gain x_search capability
  • Search real-time trends, tweets, and public sentiment
  • Example: Ask “What are people discussing about AI Agents on X today?” → Grok uses x_search to pull real-time tweets

Notes:

  • The xAI plugin now auto-enables from web-search and tool config — no manual plugin activation needed
  • openclaw onboard and openclaw configure --section web now include x_search configuration options
  • x_search uses the shared xAI key — no additional API key required

Comparison with Similar Products:

ProductxAI/Grokx_searchAuto Plugin Enable
OpenClaw✅ Responses API✅ Native✅
ZeroClaw✅ Via traits❌ Manual❌
Nanobot✅ Basic support❌❌
IronClaw✅Unknown❌

Trend: Provider-specific tools (x_search, Gemini’s Google Search) are proliferating. Runtimes need to auto-discover and enable these tools rather than requiring manual configuration. OpenClaw is ahead here.

2.2 MiniMax Image Generation + Model Cleanup (#54487)

Section titled “2.2 MiniMax Image Generation + Model Cleanup (#54487)”

Background: MiniMax is a Chinese AI company that launched the image-01 image generation model. Simultaneously, old models were cleaned up, retaining only M2.7.

Use Case:

  • Text-to-image: generate mode with aspect ratio control
  • Image-to-image: image-to-image editing mode
  • Example: Say “Generate a cyberpunk-style cat” in chat → calls MiniMax image-01

Notes:

  • Old models M2, M2.1, M2.5, VL-01 have been removed — instances configured with these models need updating
  • Domestic API access may require specific network configuration

Comparison: Most similar products don’t natively support image generation providers, relying on users to configure MCP or external tools. OpenClaw pushes further on multimodal support.

Trend: Agents aren’t just text interaction anymore — image generation/understanding is becoming a standard capability.

2.3 OpenAI apply_patch Enabled by Default

Section titled “2.3 OpenAI apply_patch Enabled by Default”

Background: apply_patch is OpenAI Codex’s code editing tool, previously requiring manual activation.

Use Case: Now available by default when using OpenAI or Codex models for code editing tasks.

Notes:

  • Sandbox policy aligned with write permissions — apply_patch permissions match file write permissions
  • Good news for ACP tasks using Codex in our cluster

Comparison: ZeroClaw and IronClaw haven’t implemented apply_patch yet. NanoClaw handles code editing inside containers due to its container isolation approach.

2.4 Mistral Request Standardization Fix

Section titled “2.4 Mistral Request Standardization Fix”

Background: Subtle differences between Mistral’s official API and OpenAI-compatible API request formats were causing 422 errors.

Use Case: Users connecting directly to Mistral’s official API (not via OpenRouter relay).

Notes: If you previously abandoned Mistral direct connection due to 422 errors, it’s worth trying again.

2.5 Google/Gemini Model Resolution Fix (#56567)

Section titled “2.5 Google/Gemini Model Resolution Fix (#56567)”

Background: Gemini 3.1’s pro/flash/flash-lite variants failed to resolve under different provider aliases, and flash-lite had prefix-matching order issues.

Use Case: Users configured with Google AI Studio, Vertex AI, or other Gemini provider aliases.

Notes: Fixed provider ID passthrough issues and added template-provider fallback. If Gemini flash-lite model switching wasn’t working before, it should be fine now.

2.6 Ollama thinking=off Fix (#53200)

Section titled “2.6 Ollama thinking=off Fix (#53200)”

Background: When thinkingLevel=off was set, Ollama models would still generate hidden reasoning tokens in the background, wasting compute and adding latency.

Use Case: Locally deployed Ollama running thinking-capable models (e.g., DeepSeek-R1, QwQ) where reasoning isn’t needed.

Notes: The fix now sends the think: false parameter. Important for resource-constrained devices — avoids unnecessary reasoning tokens.

Comparison: PicoClaw and ZeroClaw both support Ollama, but their thinking parameter control granularity doesn’t match OpenClaw’s.

2.7 Anthropic Stop Reason Handling (#56639)

Section titled “2.7 Anthropic Stop Reason Handling (#56639)”

Background: The Anthropic API sometimes returns non-standard stop reasons (e.g., sensitive — content safety block), which previously caused OpenClaw to crash.

Use Case: Any scenario using Claude models, especially when touching sensitive topics.

Notes: Now returned as a structured error instead of a crash. Important for cluster stability.

2.8 OpenAI Codex Image Tool Fix (#54829)

Section titled “2.8 OpenAI Codex Image Tool Fix (#54829)”

Background: Codex models were missing media-understanding provider registration, causing image analysis to fail.

Use Case: Using ACP to have Codex analyze screenshots, UI images, etc.

Notes: Also fixed generic image-runtime fallback (#54858), affecting third-party providers like OpenRouter and MiniMax Portal.

2.9 OpenAI WebSocket Reasoning Preservation (#53856)

Section titled “2.9 OpenAI WebSocket Reasoning Preservation (#53856)”

Background: In WebSocket mode, tool turns would lose reasoning replay metadata and tool-call item IDs, causing subsequent reasoning to break.

Use Case: Real-time interaction scenarios using OpenAI Responses API + WebSocket.

Notes: Two fixes (reasoning blocks restored + metadata kept intact) suggest this was a deep-seated issue.

2.10 GitHub Copilot Auth Refresh (#55360)

Section titled “2.10 GitHub Copilot Auth Refresh (#55360)”

Background: The expires_at value was treated as milliseconds when it was actually a seconds-level epoch, causing setTimeout to overflow and enter an infinite hot loop.

Use Case: Users running GitHub Copilot as a provider.

Notes: This was a performance bug — it would max out CPU. If you previously experienced system sluggishness after configuring Copilot, this was the cause.

2.11 Agent Model-Level Rate Limit Isolation (#49834)

Section titled “2.11 Agent Model-Level Rate Limit Isolation (#49834)”

Background: Previously, one model hitting 429 would block all models under the same auth profile.

Use Case: Configurations with multiple model fallbacks (e.g., Claude → GPT → Gemini).

Example: Claude hits 429, GPT should continue working, but previously the entire profile got cooled down.

Notes:

  • Cooldown strategy changed from exponential (1min → 1h) to stepped (30s / 1min / 5min) — more reasonable
  • New user-visible countdown messages
  • Important for heavily-used cluster instances

Comparison with Similar Products:

ProductModel-Level Rate LimitFallback ChainUser Notification

ZeroClaw✅ Trait-driven✅Basic
Nanobot❌ Simple retryLimited❌
NanoClaw❌❌❌

2.12 Codex Failover Improvements (#55206, #42892)

Section titled “2.12 Codex Failover Improvements (#55206, #42892)”

Background: Codex’s accountId token extraction failures and server_error weren’t previously treated as failover-eligible errors.

Use Case: Automatic switching when Codex fails as an ACP backend.

Notes:

  • server_error now triggers failover
  • Codex error messages are cleaned before showing to users (no more raw error payloads and request_ids)
  • context-overflow guidance preserved for invalid_request_error

2.13 Agent Model Hot-Switching

Section titled “2.13 Agent Model Hot-Switching”

Background: Switching models mid-embedded-run previously waited for the current run to finish before taking effect.

Use Case: Using /model to switch to another model when the current one is overloaded or stuck.

Notes: Now switches at the next safe retry boundary without waiting for the entire run to complete. Noticeably improves responsiveness.

2.14 HTTP 410 as Retryable Error (#55201)

Section titled “2.14 HTTP 410 as Retryable Error (#55201)”

Background: Some providers return 410 Gone to indicate temporary unavailability, but it was previously treated as a permanent error.

Notes: 410 now defaults to timeout retry, while session-expired, billing, and auth signals are still correctly identified as non-retryable.

2.15 Ollama HTTP 503 Fallback Fix (#55214)

Section titled “2.15 Ollama HTTP 503 Fallback Fix (#55214)”

Background: When Ollama returned non-2xx status codes, error messages lacked the status code prefix, preventing fallback logic from identifying them.

Use Case: Automatic switching when the local Ollama service is temporarily unavailable (e.g., model loading).

2.16 Tavily X-Client-Source Header (#55335)

Section titled “2.16 Tavily X-Client-Source Header (#55335)”

Background: Tavily (web search API) wants to identify traffic originating from OpenClaw.

Use Case: Configurations using Tavily for web search.

Notes: Purely an attribution header with no functional impact. But it indicates Tavily is paying attention to traffic volume from the OpenClaw ecosystem.

2.17 Brave Search Country Filter Fix (#55695)

Section titled “2.17 Brave Search Country Filter Fix (#55695)”

Background: The Brave Search API doesn’t support certain country codes (e.g., VN), resulting in 422 errors.

Use Case: Users in Vietnam and similar regions using Brave Search.

Notes: Unsupported countries are now normalized to ALL.

2.18 Agents/Status Context Window Query Fix (#54796, #55425)

Section titled “2.18 Agents/Status Context Window Query Fix (#54796, #55425)”

Background: Anthropic 4.6 models’ context window was displayed as the overly small shared cache minimum rather than the actual 1.0M window.

Notes: Also fixed session_status display of runtime session model and thinkingDefault.

Section titled “2.19 OpenAI-Compatible Tool Calls Deduplication (#40996)”

Notes:

  • /approve now uniformly handles both exec and plugin approvals
  • This is an architectural change that significantly improves plugin security

Section titled “3.4 Plugin Runtime Registration Isolation (#56101)”

Section titled “4.1 ACP Current-Conversation Binds”

Background: Previously, ACP spawn could only create child threads — it couldn’t directly bind to the current chat.

Use Case:

  • Launch a Codex workspace directly in the current Discord/iMessage/BlueBubbles conversation
  • Example: /acp spawn codex --bind here → the current chat becomes a Codex workspace without creating a child thread

Notes:

  • Documentation now clearly distinguishes three concepts: chat surface / ACP session / runtime workspace
  • Supported on Discord, BlueBubbles, and iMessage

Comparison: This is a feature unique to OpenClaw. Similar products don’t have the multi-channel ACP concept.

Trend: Agent integration with messaging platforms keeps deepening — from “call an agent within a chat” to “the chat itself is the agent workspace.”

Section titled “4.2 ACPX Agent Registry Alignment (#28321)”

Use Case: ACP harness routing to the wrong agent or executing unexpected commands.

Notes:

  • ⚠️ Security fix — Unknown agent IDs no longer fall through to raw command execution
  • npx built-ins pinned to exact version numbers

4.3 Agent Compaction Multiple Fixes (#49479, #51072, #46417, #45493)

Section titled “4.3 Agent Compaction Multiple Fixes (#49479, #51072, #46417, #45493)”

Background: Compaction (context compression) is a critical feature for long conversations. This release includes four related fixes:

  1. Post-compaction AGENTS refresh maintained in stale-usage preflight and queued followups
  2. Cancellation reason refinement — safeguard-specific cancel vs. manual /compact no-op distinction
  3. Timeout recovery — compress before high-context LLM timeout instead of retrying
  4. Count coordination — embedded auto-compaction success updates sessions.json

Use Case: Long-running agent sessions, especially during complex coding tasks.

Notes: #46417 is particularly important — previously, high-context timeouts would infinitely retry the same oversized request. Now it compresses first, then retries.

11. Summary: Evolutionary Trends

Section titled “11. Summary: Evolutionary Trends”

11.1 Continuous Security Hardening

Section titled “11.1 Continuous Security Hardening”
  • Plugin approval hooks (requireApproval)
  • Sandbox fine-grained control (alsoAllow + glob)
  • ACPX agent IDs no longer fall through to raw execution
  • Control UI hides sensitive config by default
  • Web search key audit scope expanded

Comparison: IronClaw (TEE) and NanoClaw (container isolation) each take a different approach to security. OpenClaw follows the “config-level fine-grained control + human-in-the-loop” path.

11.2 Channel Abstraction Maturation

Section titled “11.2 Channel Abstraction Maturation”
  • Upload-file action unified across channels
  • Numerous channel edge case fixes (loops, leaks, false triggers)
  • Deepened Matrix E2EE and Voice Bubble support
  • ACP current-conversation bind

Comparison: OpenClaw still far surpasses all competitors in channel coverage and depth. ZeroClaw is catching up in channel count but lacks deep features.

11.3 Plugin-ify Everything

Section titled “11.3 Plugin-ify Everything”
  • CLI backends → plugin surface
  • Memory flush → plugin contract
  • Heartbeat trigger → plugin API
  • Auto-load reduces manual configuration

Comparison: ZeroClaw uses traits to achieve something similar but in a more Rust-native way; Nanobot is too small for a plugin system.

11.4 Provider Ecosystem Expansion

Section titled “11.4 Provider Ecosystem Expansion”
  • xAI Responses API + x_search
  • MiniMax image generation
  • Model-level rate limit isolation
  • Better failover and error classification

Comparison: OpenClaw’s 22+ providers match ZeroClaw’s 22+ providers. Nanobot and PicoClaw have limited provider support.

11.5 Stability and Edge Cases

Section titled “11.5 Stability and Edge Cases”
  • Numerous channel-specific fixes (Telegram splitting, Discord reconnection, WhatsApp loops, Matrix encryption, etc.)
  • Multiple compaction fixes
  • Heartbeat timer recovery

Comparison: This is a unique advantage of OpenClaw as the largest-install-base project (186K+ stars, 100K+ installations) — a massive user base means more edge cases discovered and fixed. Similar products haven’t reached this scale yet.

Analysis based on the original changelog + public documentation and GitHub repos of comparable products

Claude Code 2.1.85 Deep Dive: Feature-by-Feature Analysis, Cross-Product Comparison & Evolution Trends

Mar 27, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Release Overview

Section titled “Release Overview”

2.1.85 is a “platform maturity” release — 9 new features + 17 bug fixes + 4 performance optimizations — centered on four themes: MCP ecosystem standardization, enterprise-grade hooks, terminal experience polish, and large-session stability.

New Features: Feature-by-Feature Analysis

Section titled “New Features: Feature-by-Feature Analysis”

1. MCP Multi-Server Environment Variables (CLAUDE_CODE_MCP_SERVER_NAME / CLAUDE_CODE_MCP_SERVER_URL)

Section titled “1. MCP Multi-Server Environment Variables (CLAUDE_CODE_MCP_SERVER_NAME / CLAUDE_CODE_MCP_SERVER_URL)”

Background: Previously, an MCP header helper script could only be hard-coded to serve one specific MCP server. If you had five MCP servers, you needed five nearly identical helper scripts.

Use cases:

  • An enterprise runs jira-mcp, confluence-mcp, and sentry-mcp — all of which need an OAuth Bearer token header injected in the same format
  • You can now write a single generic helper: #!/bin/bash echo "Authorization: Bearer $(get_token $CLAUDE_CODE_MCP_SERVER_NAME)"
  • At runtime, Claude Code automatically injects the current server’s name and URL

Notes: The helper script must be able to return different tokens dynamically based on server name/URL. Do not use a globally fixed value.

Cross-product comparison:

ProductMCP Header Customization
Claude CodeEnvironment variable injection — one helper serves multiple servers
Codex CLINo MCP support (OpenAI uses its own plugin system)
Gemini CLISupports MCP, but header customization is less granular than Claude Code

Trend: MCP header customization exists to accommodate enterprise authentication gateways and zero-trust network architectures. This may eventually evolve into declarative auth config (similar to Kubernetes ServiceAccount token auto-mounting).

2. Conditional Hook Execution (if Field with Permission-Rule Syntax)

Section titled “2. Conditional Hook Execution (if Field with Permission-Rule Syntax)”

Background: The previous hook system fired on everything — every PreToolUse event would fork a process to run the hook script, even if that hook only cared about git commands. Frequent process forking means added latency and wasted CPU.

Use case:

This triggers only when a git-related Bash command is executed; all other Bash calls (npm, python, etc.) are skipped outright.

Notes:

  • The if syntax reuses the permission-rule pattern-matching format (Bash(git *) means: the Bash tool, with arguments matching git *)
  • Non-matching hooks spawn no processes at all — it’s a pure string-match skip
  • Be careful with wildcard scope: Bash(rm *) will match rm -rf /

Cross-product comparison:

ProductHook Conditional Filtering
Claude Codeif condition using permission-rule syntax
Codex CLIHas a hook system but no conditional filtering; uses layered sandbox policies instead
Gemini CLINo hook system; uses coarse-grained tool policies

Trend: The hook system is evolving toward a “lightweight policy engine.” The progression goes: conditional matching → condition chains → a full declarative policy engine akin to OPA/Rego.

3. Scheduled Task Timestamp Markers (/loop and CronCreate transcript labels)

Section titled “3. Scheduled Task Timestamp Markers (/loop and CronCreate transcript labels)”

Background: When running tasks via /loop or cron, the transcript contained no record of when each execution was triggered. After the fact, there was no way to distinguish manual from automated triggers or reconstruct the timeline.

Use case:

  • You configure /loop to check CI status every 10 minutes
  • The transcript now shows entries like [2026-03-27 14:30:00 UTC — /loop triggered]
  • When reviewing a session, it’s immediately clear which actions were automated

Notes: Timestamps are in UTC. You’ll need to convert to local time manually.

Cross-product comparison:

ProductScheduled Task Auditability
Claude CodeInline timestamps embedded in the transcript
Codex CLINo built-in loop/cron mechanism
Gemini CLITask tracker was just integrated into the system prompt; no time markers yet

Trend: Auditability for AI agents is a hard requirement in enterprise procurement. This will likely evolve into OpenTelemetry span-level tracing.

4. Trailing Space After Pasted Image Placeholders ([Image #N] followed by a space)

Section titled “4. Trailing Space After Pasted Image Placeholders ([Image #N] followed by a space)”

Background: After pasting an image, the [Image #1] placeholder was immediately followed by user-typed text, causing the tokenizer to potentially merge the placeholder and the text.

Use case: After pasting a screenshot and typing “fix this CSS,” the result used to be [Image #1]fix this CSS. It now correctly produces [Image #1] fix this CSS.

Notes: A minor change, but important for the robustness of multimodal interactions.

Cross-product comparison: All three products support image pasting in similar ways. This is a polish-level detail that does not represent a competitive differentiator.

5. Deep Link Length Extended to 5,000 Characters

Section titled “5. Deep Link Length Extended to 5,000 Characters”

Background: The claude-cli://open?q=... deep link had a short character limit that prevented passing complex pre-filled prompts. CI/CD tools and IDE plugins wanting to open Claude Code with full context would have their payloads truncated.

Use cases:

  • A CI pipeline failure automatically generates a deep link: claude-cli://open?q=This%20build%20failed%20with%20error... (with the full error log attached)
  • Internal team wikis embed one-click debug links
  • Prompts that exceed a readable length display a “scroll to review” warning to prevent blind execution

Notes: The 5,000-character limit applies to the URL-encoded string; the actual content is shorter. Browsers also impose their own limits on total URL length.

Cross-product comparison:

ProductDeep Link / URL Scheme
Claude Codeclaude-cli://open?q=..., up to 5,000 characters
Codex CLINo standard deep link scheme
Gemini CLINo standard deep link scheme

Trend: Deep links are the bridge for IDE-to-CLI integration. A standardized coding agent URL scheme protocol is a likely future development.

6. MCP OAuth RFC 9728 Compliance

Section titled “6. MCP OAuth RFC 9728 Compliance”

Background: MCP OAuth previously used a custom discovery mechanism to locate the authorization server. RFC 9728 (Protected Resource Metadata), which became a standard in late 2024, defines how a resource server can advertise its associated authorization server for automatic discovery.

Use case:

  • The MCP server returns WWW-Authenticate: Bearer plus a resource_metadata URL
  • Claude Code automatically fetches that URL to retrieve authorization_server information
  • Users no longer need to manually configure the OAuth issuer, token endpoint, or other parameters

Notes:

  • The MCP server must also implement the RFC 9728 metadata endpoint
  • There may be transitional compatibility issues with the older discovery mechanism

Cross-product comparison:

ProductOAuth Standards Compliance
Claude CodeRFC 9728 discovery
Codex CLIN/A (does not use MCP OAuth)
Gemini CLIMCP support in progress; OAuth implementation details not yet public

Trend: MCP ecosystem authentication is converging from “every vendor rolling their own” toward RFC-standard flows. This is critical for enterprise SSO integration.

7. Organization Policy Blocks Plugin Installation (managed-settings.json)

Section titled “7. Organization Policy Blocks Plugin Installation (managed-settings.json)”

Background: Enterprise IT teams need control over which plugins can be installed. Previously, managed-settings.json could flag blocked plugins, but those plugins remained visible in the marketplace — users could see them but not install them, creating a confusing experience.

Use case: A company’s security policy prohibits all third-party shell-execution plugins. Those plugins now disappear entirely from the marketplace, so employees never encounter the confusing “why can’t I install this?” situation.

Notes: This is an organization-level setting and does not affect individual users. IT admins must maintain managed-settings.json.

Cross-product comparison:

ProductEnterprise Plugin Management
Claude Codemanaged-settings.json + marketplace hiding
Codex CLIProduct-scoped plugin sync just landed in v0.117
Gemini CLIHas a settings.json policy but no marketplace integration

Trend: All three vendors are accelerating enterprise control capabilities. The end state will likely align with MDM (Mobile Device Management)-level policy distribution.

8. PreToolUse Hook Satisfying AskUserQuestion (Headless Integration)

Section titled “8. PreToolUse Hook Satisfying AskUserQuestion (Headless Integration)”

Background: When Claude Code needs to ask the user a question (AskUserQuestion) in a headless or CI environment, there is no human available to respond. Previously, execution would simply time out and fail.

Use case:

The hook script returns {"permissionDecision": "allow", "updatedInput": "Yes, proceed with the refactor"}, automatically answering on behalf of the user.

This enables Claude Code to run fully unattended:

  • Automatically fixing lint issues in CI/CD
  • Batch refactoring tasks
  • Bridging user Q&A through a Slack bot

Notes:

  • Design the auto-answer logic carefully to avoid automatically saying “yes” when the agent is about to perform a dangerous operation
  • Pairing this with if conditional filtering is recommended so that only specific question types are auto-answered

Cross-product comparison:

ProductHeadless Auto-Response
Claude CodeHook returns updatedInput
Codex CLISupports --yes for global auto-approval, but without fine-grained control
Gemini CLINo comparable mechanism

Trend: This is a key piece of the “Agent-as-a-Service” puzzle. A complete Human-in-the-Loop API with routing to Slack/Teams/webhooks is a likely future development.

9. OTEL tool_parameters Gating (OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1)

Section titled “9. OTEL tool_parameters Gating (OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1)”

Background: tool_result events in OpenTelemetry traces include tool parameters by default, which can expose sensitive information — API keys, file contents, and so on — to monitoring systems.

Use case:

  • Production environments default to off: tool parameters are not recorded in OTEL logs
  • When debugging, set OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1 to enable full parameter logging

Notes: The default behavior has changed. Previously, parameters were always logged. Now they are not logged by default. If your monitoring pipeline depends on this data, you must opt in explicitly.

Cross-product comparison:

ProductOTEL Privacy Control
Claude CodeEnvironment variable gating
Codex CLISupports OTEL but no fine-grained gating
Gemini CLINo OTEL integration yet

Trend: Observability and privacy compliance are two sides of the same coin. Field-level redaction standards for OTEL are a likely future development.

Bug Fixes: Fix-by-Fix Analysis

Section titled “Bug Fixes: Fix-by-Fix Analysis”

Fix 1: /compact Fails on Oversized Conversations (“context exceeded”)

Section titled “Fix 1: /compact Fails on Oversized Conversations (“context exceeded”)”

Background: The /compact command works by sending the conversation to the LLM for summarization. When the conversation has grown so large that even the compact request itself exceeds the context window, execution enters a deadlock — it’s too large and needs compacting, but the compact operation itself is also too large to run.

Resolution: Likely implemented as a segmented compression approach or a truncate-then-compact strategy.

Cross-product comparison: Codex’s compaction now runs in the background to reduce UI blocking (see performance comparison below). Gemini CLI has no equivalent feature.

Fixes 2–3: Plugin Enable/Disable Path Mismatch & Worktree Error in Non-Git Repositories

Section titled “Fixes 2–3: Plugin Enable/Disable Path Mismatch & Worktree Error in Non-Git Repositories”

Background:

  • When the declared plugin location (in settings) and the actual installation location differ, enable/disable operations cannot find the file
  • Using --worktree in a non-git directory caused an immediate crash before the WorktreeCreate hook could even run

Cross-product note: Codex v0.117 also recently fixed a plugin gating-related bug.

Fix 4: deniedMcpServers Not Blocking claude.ai MCP Servers

Section titled “Fix 4: deniedMcpServers Not Blocking claude.ai MCP Servers”

Background: The deniedMcpServers security setting only blocked MCP servers configured through the CLI, not those passed through from the claude.ai web interface. This was a security vulnerability — the enterprise-configured blocklist could be bypassed.

Cross-product note: This is a Claude Code-specific issue, as it is the only product that connects to both CLI and web MCP sources simultaneously.

Fix 5: switch_display Not Working in Multi-Monitor Setups

Section titled “Fix 5: switch_display Not Working in Multi-Monitor Setups”

Background: The Computer Use tool’s switch_display action was returning “not available” in multi-monitor environments. Multi-monitor configurations are common in enterprise settings where computer use automation is relevant.

Cross-product note: Codex and Gemini CLI do not have built-in computer use capabilities.

Fix 6: Crash When OTEL Exporter Is Set to none

Section titled “Fix 6: Crash When OTEL Exporter Is Set to none”

Background: Setting OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER=none to disable log export caused the program to crash. This was a straightforward null-value handling bug.

Fix 7: Diff Syntax Highlighting Broken in Non-Native Builds

Section titled “Fix 7: Diff Syntax Highlighting Broken in Non-Native Builds”

Background: Non-native builds packaged via pkg/bun were missing the tree-sitter WASM bindings.

Fix 8: MCP Step-Up Authorization Failure (When a Refresh Token Is Present)

Section titled “Fix 8: MCP Step-Up Authorization Failure (When a Refresh Token Is Present)”

Background: OAuth includes a “step-up auth” scenario where the user is already logged in but the server requires elevated permissions (for example, accessing sensitive data requires MFA). The server returns 403 insufficient_scope. When a refresh token is already present locally, the code incorrectly attempted to refresh rather than re-authenticate.

Example: An MCP server requires scope: admin:write, but the local token only has scope: read. The server returns 403. Claude Code should prompt for re-authorization rather than looping with the old refresh token.

Trend: As MCP servers integrate with enterprise IAM systems, step-up auth scenarios will become increasingly common.

Fixes 9–10: Remote Session Memory Leak & Persistent ECONNRESET Errors

Section titled “Fixes 9–10: Remote Session Memory Leak & Persistent ECONNRESET Errors”

Background:

  • In remote sessions, when a streaming response was interrupted, the response buffer was not released, causing memory to grow indefinitely
  • The edge connection layer was repeatedly retrying the same broken TCP connection on instability; this has been changed so each retry uses a fresh TCP connection

Cross-product note: Codex v0.117 also fixed similar stability issues in remote multi-agent sessions.

Fixes 11–15: Terminal Interaction & Input Handling

Section titled “Fixes 11–15: Terminal Interaction & Input Handling”
BugDescription
Prompt queue getting stuckAfter a slash command, the prompt gets stuck in the queue and cannot be recalled with the up arrow
Python SDK MCP servers missingMCP servers of type:'sdk' were being filtered out at startup
Raw key sequences in SSH/VSCodeTerminal sequences were not parsed correctly, causing garbled output
Remote Control stuck at “Requires Action”Status not updated after permission was resolved
shift+enter intercepted by typeaheadAttempting to insert a newline gets swallowed by autocomplete suggestions

Fixes 16–17: Scrolling and Terminal Exit

Section titled “Fixes 16–17: Scrolling and Terminal Exit”
BugDescription
Flickering when scrolling up during streaming outputStale content bleeding into the visible area
Keyboard protocol not restored after exiting Ghostty/Kitty/WezTermAfter quitting Claude Code, Ctrl+C and Ctrl+D stop working

Kitty keyboard protocol issue in detail: The Kitty keyboard protocol is an enhanced keyboard mode for modern terminals. Claude Code enabled enhanced mode on entry but did not send the CSI ? u reset sequence on exit. This left the terminal in enhanced mode, causing all keyboard shortcuts to behave abnormally.

Cross-product note: Codex v0.117 also fixed a similar terminal state restoration bug (Shift+Left shortcut in tmux). This is a common problem for all terminal TUI applications.

Performance Optimizations

Section titled “Performance Optimizations”

1. @-mention File Autocomplete Performance (Large Repositories)

Section titled “1. @-mention File Autocomplete Performance (Large Repositories)”

Background: Typing @ to trigger file autocomplete in a monorepo with tens of thousands of files previously caused noticeable lag or timeouts.

Cross-product note: Codex v0.117 also made significant UI responsiveness improvements in the app-server TUI.

2. Improved Dangerous Command Detection for PowerShell

Section titled “2. Improved Dangerous Command Detection for PowerShell”

Background: The previous PowerShell command allowlist/blocklist was incomplete, allowing some obfuscated dangerous commands — such as iex, an alias for Invoke-Expression — to evade detection.

3. Large Transcript Scrolling Performance (yoga-layout replaced with pure TypeScript)

Section titled “3. Large Transcript Scrolling Performance (yoga-layout replaced with pure TypeScript)”

Background: The TUI was using the WASM build of yoga-layout (Facebook’s Flexbox engine) for layout computation. The WASM bridge introduces serialization overhead that becomes a bottleneck when transcript content is large. Replacing it with a pure TypeScript implementation eliminates the cross-language call overhead.

Cross-product note: Codex enabled app-server TUI by default in v0.117, using a fundamentally different performance architecture (client-server separation).

4. UI Blocking During Large-Session Compaction

Section titled “4. UI Blocking During Large-Session Compaction”

Background: Compaction (context compression) is a CPU-intensive operation. Running it on the main thread freezes the UI.

Three-Product Comprehensive Comparison

Section titled “Three-Product Comprehensive Comparison”
DimensionClaude Code 2.1.85Codex CLI v0.117Gemini CLI v0.34
Hook SystemConditional filtering + headless auto-responseBasic hooksNone
MCP SupportRFC 9728 OAuth + multi-server headersProprietary plugin systemBasic MCP
Plugin EcosystemMarketplace + enterprise managementFirst-class status just introducedNo marketplace
Multi-AgentPrimarily single-agentMulti-agent v2 (path-based addressing)Local subagent execution + tool isolation
Enterprise Controlsmanaged-settings + plugin blockingProduct-scoped policiessettings.json policy
ObservabilityOTEL + privacy gatingBasic OTELNo OTEL
Terminal CompatibilityNumerous terminal bugs fixed this releaseTerminal state restoration fixedTerminal compatibility average
Scheduled Tasks/loop + CronCreateNone built-inTask tracker just integrated
Deep Link5,000 charactersNoneNone
Architecture DirectionHook + MCP platformizationRust rewrite + app-server separationSubagent + A2A protocol

Future Evolution Trends

Section titled “Future Evolution Trends”

1. Standardization of Agent Collaboration Layer

Section titled “1. Standardization of Agent Collaboration Layer”
  • Codex already has multi-agent v2 (path-based addressing: /root/agent_a)
  • Gemini is pushing the A2A (Agent-to-Agent) protocol with agent acknowledgment
  • Claude Code is primarily single-agent for now, but the hook system and headless capabilities are laying the groundwork for agent orchestration
  • Prediction: All three vendors will converge on some form of A2A or MCP agent-layer interoperability standard within 2026

2. From CLI to Platform

Section titled “2. From CLI to Platform”
  • Codex’s app-server architecture (WebSocket + remote TUI) is already not a traditional CLI
  • Claude Code’s deep link and remote session features are also moving in a platform direction
  • Prediction: Terminal coding agents will ultimately evolve into headless coding services with multiple frontends (CLI / IDE / Web / API)

3. Accelerating Enterprise Security Compliance

Section titled “3. Accelerating Enterprise Security Compliance”
  • All three vendors are adding managed settings and policy engines
  • OTEL observability is becoming a standard enterprise requirement
  • Prediction: SOC 2 and FedRAMP compliance certifications will become competitive moats for coding agent products

4. Hook System → Policy Engine → Agent Guardrails

Section titled “4. Hook System → Policy Engine → Agent Guardrails”
  • The if condition in Claude Code hooks is just the beginning
  • Prediction: This will eventually evolve into declarative policies (similar to OPA) supporting complex condition chains, approval workflows, and automatic rollbacks

5. MCP Ecosystem Explosion

Section titled “5. MCP Ecosystem Explosion”
  • RFC 9728 compliance = enterprise SSO integration unblocked
  • Step-up auth fix = support for tiered permissions in enterprise IAM
  • Prediction: MCP becomes the “HTTP” of AI agents — a universal tool-calling protocol. Claude Code currently leads on compliance

In one sentence: Claude Code 2.1.85 is an “enterprise-grade polish” release — not chasing flashy new capabilities, but making existing capabilities genuinely production-ready in enterprise environments. By comparison, Codex is more aggressive in architectural reconstruction (Rust + app-server), while Gemini is more aggressive in multi-agent collaboration. All three are taking different paths toward the same destination: a headless, observable, policy-governed coding agent platform.

Claude Code 2.1.83 Changelog: Item-by-Item Deep Analysis

Mar 25, 2026
Vibe Sparking

I. New Features (Added)

Section titled “I. New Features (Added)”

1. managed-settings.d/ Drop-in Policy Directory

Section titled “1. managed-settings.d/ Drop-in Policy Directory”

Added managed-settings.d/ drop-in directory alongside managed-settings.json, letting separate teams deploy independent policy fragments that merge alphabetically

Enterprise deployment pattern: security team deploys 00-security.json (block curl/wget), platform team deploys 10-platform.json (internal MCP servers), business team deploys 20-team-alpha.json (custom Hooks). Files merge alphabetically by filename, numeric prefixes control priority. Similar to Linux’s /etc/sudoers.d/ pattern.

Trend: From single-file → drop-in directory management, the standard pattern for multi-team enterprise collaboration.

2. CwdChanged and FileChanged Hook Events

Section titled “2. CwdChanged and FileChanged Hook Events”

Added CwdChanged and FileChanged hook events for reactive environment management (e.g., direnv)

When Claude switches directories in a monorepo, CwdChanged can auto-run direnv allow to load that directory’s env vars. FileChanged triggers when .env files are modified. Hook events continue to evolve: lifecycle events → tool events → now environment events.

3. sandbox.failIfUnavailable Setting

Section titled “3. sandbox.failIfUnavailable Setting”

Added sandbox.failIfUnavailable setting to exit with an error when sandbox is enabled but cannot start, instead of running unsandboxed

Previously, if sandbox dependencies were missing, Claude Code would silently fall back to unsandboxed execution — a serious security gap. Now enterprises can enforce hard-fail when sandbox can’t start.

Trend: Security policy evolving from “default permissive” → “optionally strict” → eventually “strict by default”.

4. disableDeepLinkRegistration Setting

Section titled “4. disableDeepLinkRegistration Setting”

Added disableDeepLinkRegistration setting to prevent claude-cli:// protocol handler registration

For Docker containers, CI/CD pipelines, and locked-down enterprise environments where protocol handler registration is unnecessary or harmful.

5. CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1

Section titled “5. CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1”

Added CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1 to strip Anthropic and cloud provider credentials from subprocess environments

Prevents malicious prompt injection from stealing API keys via env/printenv. Strips Anthropic + cloud provider (AWS_, GCP_, AZURE_*) credentials from Bash tools, hooks, and MCP stdio servers.

Trend: Supply chain security in AI toolchains. Expected to become default-on in the future.

6. Transcript Search

Section titled “6. Transcript Search”

Added transcript search — press / in transcript mode (Ctrl+O) to search, n/N to step through matches

vim/less-style search in conversation history. Essential for long sessions with hundreds of turns.

7. Ctrl+X Ctrl+E External Editor

Section titled “7. Ctrl+X Ctrl+E External Editor”

Added Ctrl+X Ctrl+E as an alias for opening the external editor (readline-native binding)

Standard readline keybinding for opening $EDITOR. Ctrl+G still works. Aligns with bash/zsh muscle memory.

8. Pasted Image [Image #N] Chips

Section titled “8. Pasted Image [Image #N] Chips”

Pasted images now insert an [Image #N] chip at the cursor so you can reference them positionally

Paste two UI screenshots, type: “Compare the navbar in [Image #1] with [Image #2] and identify differences.”

Trend: Multimodal interaction refinement — from “look at this” to “precisely reference this image”.

9. Agent initialPrompt in Frontmatter

Section titled “9. Agent initialPrompt in Frontmatter”

Agents can now declare initialPrompt in frontmatter to auto-submit a first turn

Agents start executing immediately without waiting for user input. Useful for code review agents that should analyze the current diff on launch.

10. Keybinding Rebinding

Section titled “10. Keybinding Rebinding”

chat:killAgents and chat:fastMode are now rebindable via ~/.claude/keybindings.json

Resolves conflicts with tmux, screen, and other terminal multiplexers.

II. Bug Fixes (Fixed)

Section titled “II. Bug Fixes (Fixed)”

Security Fixes

Section titled “Security Fixes”
  • #17: Fixed --mcp-config CLI flag bypassing allowedMcpServers/deniedMcpServers managed policy enforcement — enterprise users should upgrade immediately
  • #18: Fixed caffeinate process not terminating on exit, preventing Mac from sleeping

Stability Fixes

Section titled “Stability Fixes”
  • #11: Fixed mouse tracking escape sequences leaking to shell after exit
  • #12: Fixed Claude Code hanging on exit on macOS
  • #13: Fixed screen flashing blank after idle
  • #14: Fixed hang when diffing very large files — now times out after 5 seconds with graceful fallback
  • #15: Fixed 1-8 second UI freeze on startup when voice input enabled (lazy loading fix)
  • #16: Fixed ~3s startup regression from claude.ai MCP config fetch (now async)

Context & Agent Fixes

Section titled “Context & Agent Fixes”
  • #22: Fixed background subagents becoming invisible after context compaction, causing duplicate agent spawns — critical for multi-agent workflows
  • #23: Fixed background agent tasks stuck in “running” state when git/API calls hang during cleanup
  • #29: Fixed SDK session history loss on resume caused by hook progress/attachment messages forking the parentUuid chain

TUI & UX Fixes

Section titled “TUI & UX Fixes”
  • #20: Fixed bash mode not activating when tab-accepting !-prefixed suggestions
  • #21: Fixed stale slash command selection showing wrong highlighted command
  • #26: Fixed queued commands flickering during streaming responses
  • #27: Fixed slash commands sent as text when submitted during message processing
  • #28: Fixed scrollback jumping when collapsed groups finish offscreen; fixed jump to top when model starts/stops thinking
  • #31: Fixed ghost characters in height-constrained lists
  • #32: Fixed Ctrl+B interfering with readline backward-char at idle prompt
  • #33: Fixed tool result files never being cleaned up (ignoring cleanupPeriodDays)

Voice & Input Fixes

Section titled “Voice & Input Fixes”
  • #34: Fixed space key swallowed for up to 3s after voice hold-to-talk release
  • #35: Fixed ALSA errors corrupting TUI on Linux without audio hardware (Docker/headless/WSL1)
  • #36: Fixed voice SoX detection on Termux/Android (kernel-restricted which)
  • #68: Fixed CJK IME full-width space not triggering voice hold-to-talk

Remote & MCP Fixes

Section titled “Remote & MCP Fixes”
  • #19: Fixed claude.ai MCP connectors unavailable in --print mode
  • #24: Fixed --channels showing error on first launch after upgrade
  • #37: Fixed Remote Control sessions showing Idle while actively running
  • #38: Fixed memory leak in remote sessions (tool use IDs accumulate indefinitely)
  • #63: Fixed MCP SSE tool calls hanging indefinitely when connection drops
  • #65: Fixed remote sessions forgetting history after container restart
  • #66: Fixed remote sessions requiring re-login on transient auth errors
  • #67: Fixed piped commands (rg | wc -l) hanging in Linux sandbox

III. Performance Improvements

Section titled “III. Performance Improvements”
  • #39: Bedrock SDK cold-start latency reduced by overlapping profile fetch
  • #40: --resume memory usage and startup latency improved for large sessions
  • #41: Plugin startup cached — commands, skills, agents load from disk cache
  • #44: WebFetch peak memory reduced for large pages
  • #45: Scrollback resets reduced from once per turn to once per ~50 messages
  • #46: claude -p startup ~600ms faster with unauthenticated MCP servers
  • #48: Non-streaming fallback cap raised (21k→64k tokens, 120s→300s timeout)
  • #49: Interrupting before response auto-restores your input
  • #50: /status now works during streaming responses
  • #59: --bare -p (SDK pattern) ~14% faster to API request

IV. Changes & Deprecations

Section titled “IV. Changes & Deprecations”
  • #43: WebFetch now identifies as Claude-User for robots.txt compliance
  • #53: “Stop all background agents” changed from Ctrl+F to Ctrl+X Ctrl+K to stop shadowing readline forward-char
  • #54: TaskOutput tool deprecated in favor of Read on the task’s output file path
  • #56: Plugin manifest.userConfig externalized — sensitive values stored in macOS Keychain or protected credentials file
  • #58: Ctrl+L now clears screen and forces full redraw (recovery from Cmd+K blanking)
  • #60: MEMORY.md index now truncates at 25KB as well as 200 lines
  • #61: AskUserQuestion and plan-mode disabled when --channels is active

V. VSCode Extension

Section titled “V. VSCode Extension”
  • #70: Spinner turns red with “Not responding” after 60s backend silence
  • #71: Fixed session history not loading on reopen via URL or restart
  • #72: Esc-twice (or /rewind) opens keyboard-navigable rewind picker
  • #73: Fixed Fork/Rewind failing silently after session cache goes stale

VI. Trend Analysis

Section titled “VI. Trend Analysis”
  1. Security defense-in-depth: sandbox.failIfUnavailable, env scrubbing, MCP policy bypass fix → evolving from optional to mandatory
  2. Startup performance is the core battlefield: 8+ startup optimizations in this release alone
  3. Message chain integrity remains structurally hard: parentUuid chain breaks causing resume failures, history loss, invisible subagents across multiple versions
  4. readline keybinding regression: Stopped hijacking Ctrl+B/F/X, moving to chords and context-aware triggers
  5. Remote/cloud sessions maturing: State sync, memory leaks, auth retry, title generation
  6. Plugin ecosystem standardizing: userConfig, MCP dedup, disk cache, immediate uninstall
  7. Multimodal interaction refinement: Image position chips, disk path references, voice fixes across edge cases

Analysis based on Claude Code 2.1.83 Changelog, official documentation (code.claude.com/docs), and historical changelog context.

Claude Code 2.1.81: --bare Mode, Mobile Approvals, and YOLO Mode

Mar 21, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Claude Code 2.1.81: —bare Mode, Mobile Approvals, and YOLO Mode

Section titled “Claude Code 2.1.81: —bare Mode, Mobile Approvals, and YOLO Mode”

2.1.81 doesn’t have any big features—just two noteworthy new flags and a pile of fixes for bugs that quietly bite you in ways you can never quite pin down. Read through each one and you’ll realize this release targets the hardest-to-notice friction in the toolchain.

Two New Flags

Section titled “Two New Flags”

--bare: Scripting Mode, Zero Overhead

Section titled “--bare: Scripting Mode, Zero Overhead”

You’re calling Claude Code with -p in CI or batch scripts, but every time you have to wait for hooks, LSP, plugin sync, and skill directory scanning. All of that makes sense in interactive mode; in an automation pipeline it’s pure waste.

--bare skips all of it:

A few conditions apply: you must provide your key via ANTHROPIC_API_KEY or apiKeyHelper in --settings—OAuth and keychain auth are unavailable in this mode. Auto-memory is also completely disabled.

The use cases are clear-cut: production pipelines, cron jobs, bulk code reviews. Anywhere you don’t need a persistent session, use --bare.

--channels: Tool Approvals Forwarded to Your Phone

Section titled “--channels: Tool Approvals Forwarded to Your Phone”

This feature requires a channel server that supports the permission capability. When that’s in place, Claude’s approval prompts for tool execution no longer block the terminal—they get sent to your phone instead.

You’re in a meeting, away from your desk, and the agent hits a step that needs confirmation. It pops up on your phone; one tap and it continues. No need to walk back to your desk.

For anyone who needs to remotely supervise an agent, this beats everything else.

Bug Fixes: A Dozen Hard-to-Explain Issues

Section titled “Bug Fixes: A Dozen Hard-to-Explain Issues”

Multi-Session OAuth Re-authentication

Section titled “Multi-Session OAuth Re-authentication”

When multiple Claude Code sessions are running simultaneously and one refreshes the OAuth token, the others would be forced to re-authenticate. Now token refreshes no longer affect other sessions.

Running multiple sessions at once is a normal workflow, and this bug would constantly interrupt you in exactly that scenario.

Two Silent Failures in Voice Mode

Section titled “Two Silent Failures in Voice Mode”
  • Retry failures would swallow the error and only show “check your network connection”—now the actual error is displayed.
  • After the server silently dropped a WebSocket connection, audio wouldn’t recover—now it automatically reconnects.

Silent failures are the hardest bugs to debug. You think it’s a network issue when really the tool is lying to you.

CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_EXPERIMENTAL_BETAS Not Working

Section titled “CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_EXPERIMENTAL_BETAS Not Working”

Even with this environment variable set, the structured-outputs beta header was still being sent. Proxy gateways forwarding to Vertex or Bedrock would return 400 because of it.

People actually using this variable had been getting proxy errors without knowing why. Fixed now.

Hyphens in Bash Command Strings Triggering Permission Prompts

Section titled “Hyphens in Bash Command Strings Triggering Permission Prompts”

String arguments containing hyphens (-) in commands would incorrectly trigger permission prompts. A command that should have run silently would instead require manual confirmation. These false alarms erode trust in the tool. Fixed.

Plugin Directory Deleted Mid-Session Causing Blocks

Section titled “Plugin Directory Deleted Mid-Session Causing Blocks”

If the plugin directory got deleted during a session, all subsequent submissions would hang. Plugin hooks no longer block prompt submission.

Race Condition in Background Task Output

Section titled “Race Condition in Background Task Output”

When a background agent task completed between two polling intervals, the output would hang forever. Fixed.

Worktree Session Restoration

Section titled “Worktree Session Restoration”

Restoring a session that was in a worktree now automatically switches back to that worktree. Previously it wouldn’t, and you’d have to cd manually.

/btw Dropping Pasted Content

Section titled “/btw Dropping Pasted Content”

Using /btw during an active response would fail to include the pasted text. Fixed.

Clipboard Race Condition in tmux

Section titled “Clipboard Race Condition in tmux”

Quickly Cmd+Tabbing and then pasting would sometimes paste stale content. The clipboard copy in tmux hadn’t finished before it was read. Fixed.

Several Remote Control Fixes

Section titled “Several Remote Control Fixes”
  • Session titles were always generic names—now they’re derived from the first prompt.
  • /rename didn’t sync the title for Remote Control sessions—now it does.
  • /exit couldn’t reliably archive sessions—now it can.
  • Titles auto-refresh after the third message.

Other

Section titled “Other”
  • Terminal tab titles not updating—fixed.
  • Invisible hook attachments inflating the message count in transcript mode—fixed.

A Few Improvements

Section titled “A Few Improvements”

MCP tool calls collapsed into a single line. Read/search calls used to expand every time; now they’re merged into “Queried {server}”, expandable with Ctrl+O. Cuts down on visual noise quite a bit.

! bash mode is more discoverable. When you need to run an interactive command, Claude now proactively mentions this mode exists. No more digging through docs.

Ref-tracked plugins re-clone on every load. Ensures you get the latest version, not a stale cache.

Plan mode hides the “clear context” option by default. To bring it back, add "showClearContextOnPlanAccept": true.

MCP OAuth supports CIMD / SEP-991. For servers without Dynamic Client Registration, you can now use Client ID Metadata Document for OAuth.

Windows (including WSL in Windows Terminal) disables line-by-line streaming output. Due to rendering issues. WSL in Windows Terminal is also affected.

[VSCode] Windows PATH inheritance fix. The PATH inheritance for the Bash tool when using Git Bash had a regression in v2.1.78—now fixed.

The Last Two Words

Section titled “The Last Two Words”

YOLO mode.

As always.

References

Section titled “References”
  • Claude Code Changelog
  • Claude Code Documentation

Claude Code 2.1.80: --channels Lets MCP Servers Push Messages Into Your Session

Mar 20, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Claude Code 2.1.80: —channels Lets MCP Servers Push Messages Into Your Session

Section titled “Claude Code 2.1.80: —channels Lets MCP Servers Push Messages Into Your Session”

A Claude Code session has always been a conversation: you talk, the agent responds. MCP servers extended that — the agent could call external tools. But information only flowed one way, outward. The agent asked questions; servers answered them.

2.1.80 opens the reverse channel. --channels (research preview) lets MCP servers push messages into your running session. The tool that could only speak when spoken to just learned to raise its hand.

At a glance

Section titled “At a glance”
AreaWhat changed
Channels--channels (research preview) lets MCP servers push messages into your session
Skillseffort frontmatter for skills and slash commands overrides model effort level
Statuslinerate_limits field in statusline scripts shows Claude.ai usage (5-hour and 7-day windows)
Pluginssource: 'settings' declares plugin entries inline in settings.json
Plugin tipsCLI tool usage detection added alongside file pattern matching
ResumeFixed --resume dropping parallel tool results — no more [Tool result missing]
VoiceFixed WebSocket failures from Cloudflare bot detection on non-browser TLS fingerprints
APIFixed 400 errors with fine-grained tool streaming through API proxies, Bedrock, Vertex
RemoteFixed /remote-control appearing where it can’t function (gateway/third-party providers)
SandboxFixed /sandbox tab switching not responding to Tab or arrow keys
UXFaster @ file autocomplete in large repos; improved /effort, /permissions navigation
Performance~80MB memory savings on startup in 250k-file repos
SettingsFixed managed settings not applied at startup when remote-settings.json was cached
PluginsSimplified plugin install tips to single /plugin install command

The channel opens both ways

Section titled “The channel opens both ways”

MCP has been a one-way street. Your agent calls a tool, the server responds. That’s it. If something happens on the server side — a CI build fails, a deployment completes, a test suite finishes — the server has no way to tell the agent. You have to ask.

--channels changes this. An MCP server can now push a message into your active session without waiting to be called. Think about what that enables:

A deployment monitor MCP server watching your staging environment. Your agent is writing code. The deploy fails. The server pushes “deploy failed: missing env var DATABASE_URL on staging” directly into the session. The agent sees it, checks the config, fixes it.

A test runner MCP server that pushes results as they complete. Your agent doesn’t have to poll. It gets notified.

A team communication MCP server that pushes relevant Slack messages or PR review comments into your coding session.

This is a research preview, meaning the API surface may change. But the direction is clear: MCP is becoming a bidirectional messaging layer, not just a tool-calling protocol.

Skills learn to set their own pace

Section titled “Skills learn to set their own pace”

effort frontmatter in skills and slash commands lets the skill author override the model’s effort level when the skill is invoked.

Before this, effort was a global setting. You’d set it high for complex work, low for quick tasks, and toggle back and forth. Now the skill decides. A code formatting command runs at minimal effort because it doesn’t need deep reasoning. An architecture review skill demands maximum effort because shortcuts produce bad analysis.

This is a small YAML field with outsized impact. Skill authors can now design for the right level of reasoning rather than hoping the user has their effort setting dialed correctly.

Rate limits, visible

Section titled “Rate limits, visible”

rate_limits is a new field available to statusline scripts. It exposes Claude.ai’s 5-hour and 7-day usage windows with used_percentage and resets_at.

If you’ve ever been surprised by hitting a rate limit mid-task, this is the fix. Your statusline can now show something like “73% of 5h limit used, resets in 2h”. No more guessing.

This only applies to Claude.ai billing. API users with their own keys have different limits.

Plugins, declared inline

Section titled “Plugins, declared inline”

source: 'settings' is a new plugin marketplace source that lets you declare plugin entries directly in settings.json. No registry lookup, no install step. Write the plugin definition in your settings file, it’s loaded.

For teams that distribute internal plugins, this simplifies distribution. Push the settings.json change, everyone gets the plugin.

Combined with CLI tool usage detection for plugin tips (alongside existing file pattern matching), the plugin discovery story is getting smarter. Claude Code can now suggest plugins based on what CLI tools you’re running, not just what files exist in your project.

The resume fix that matters more than it sounds

Section titled “The resume fix that matters more than it sounds”

--resume was dropping parallel tool results. If your previous session had parallel tool calls, resuming it would show [Tool result missing] placeholders instead of the actual results.

This is worse than it sounds. Parallel tool calls are common in complex sessions — the agent reads multiple files at once, runs tests in parallel, searches across directories simultaneously. Losing those results on resume meant the agent lost context about what it had already done. It would re-read files, re-run searches, or worse, make decisions based on incomplete information.

Fixed. All tool_use/tool_result pairs now restore correctly.

Voice mode and API fixes

Section titled “Voice mode and API fixes”

Voice mode WebSocket connections were failing because Cloudflare’s bot detection was rejecting non-browser TLS fingerprints. Claude Code’s WebSocket client doesn’t look like a browser, so Cloudflare flagged it. Fixed by adjusting the TLS fingerprint handling.

Fine-grained tool streaming was returning 400 errors when used through API proxies, Bedrock, or Vertex. If you’re running Claude Code through enterprise infrastructure, this was likely hitting you. Fixed.

/remote-control was appearing in the command list for gateway and third-party provider deployments where it can’t actually function. Removed from those contexts.

Performance: 80MB lighter on large repos

Section titled “Performance: 80MB lighter on large repos”

Startup memory usage dropped by approximately 80MB on repositories with around 250,000 files. That’s a meaningful reduction. On a machine with 16GB of RAM running multiple Claude Code instances across different repos, this gives back roughly half a gigabyte.

The @ file autocomplete in large git repositories is also more responsive now. In repos with tens of thousands of files, there was a noticeable delay when typing @ to reference a file. Reduced.

UI polish

Section titled “UI polish”

Several navigation and display improvements:

/effort now shows what “auto” currently resolves to, matching the status bar indicator. Before, selecting “auto” gave you no feedback about what effort level was actually being used.

/permissions gained proper Tab and arrow key navigation within lists. Combined with the Tab/arrow fix for /sandbox, keyboard-driven navigation is now consistent across settings panels.

The background tasks panel responds to left arrow to close from the list view.

Plugin install tips simplified from a two-step flow to a single /plugin install command.

The settings fix you didn’t know you needed

Section titled “The settings fix you didn’t know you needed”

Managed settings — enabledPlugins, permissions.defaultMode, and policy-set environment variables — weren’t being applied at startup when remote-settings.json was cached from a prior session. If your organization manages Claude Code settings centrally, this meant fresh sessions could start with stale configuration.

This is the kind of bug that’s hard to diagnose because it’s intermittent. It only happens when the cached settings are different from the current ones. Fixed.

What this release signals

Section titled “What this release signals”

--channels is a research preview, but research previews in Claude Code have a track record of becoming stable features within a few releases. The fact that it shipped means the underlying architecture is ready.

The pattern across 2.1.80 is Claude Code becoming infrastructure rather than just a tool. Channels make it a message bus. Effort frontmatter makes skills self-describing. Rate limit visibility makes it observable. Inline plugin declarations make it configurable without external dependencies.

Each of these alone is a nice improvement. Together, they’re building blocks for something that looks less like a CLI and more like a development platform.

Update with claude update. If you build MCP servers, --channels is worth experimenting with now. If you write skills, add effort frontmatter. If you’ve been flying blind on rate limits, configure your statusline.

Claude Code 2.1.79: /remote-control -- Your AI Coding Session Just Left the Terminal

Mar 19, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Claude Code 2.1.79: /remote-control — Your AI Coding Session Just Left the Terminal

Section titled “Claude Code 2.1.79: /remote-control — Your AI Coding Session Just Left the Terminal”

You’re deep in a debug session. The agent is tracing a race condition across three files, context is loaded, and you can feel the fix coming together. Then your phone buzzes. You need to step out.

Before today, that meant abandoning your session or hoping it finishes before you get back. With 2.1.79, you type /remote-control. A link appears. You open it on your phone. Your entire session — context, agent state, everything — is right there in claude.ai/code.

You walk out the door. The agent keeps working. You watch from your phone.

At a glance

Section titled “At a glance”
AreaWhat changed
Remote/remote-control bridges your terminal session to claude.ai/code — continue from browser or phone (VS Code)
Session UXSession tabs get AI-generated titles based on your first message (VS Code)
Observability”Show turn duration” toggle in /config menu
Auth--console flag for claude auth login enables Anthropic Console (API billing) authentication
Plugins${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA} for persistent state; /plugin uninstall prompts before deleting data
PerformanceStartup memory usage reduced by ~18MB
APINon-streaming fallback gets 2-minute per-attempt timeout (no more indefinite hangs)
PluginsCLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_SEED_DIR supports multiple seed directories
Bug fixes11 fixes across subprocess handling, voice mode, permissions UI, session hooks, and more

The line that changes everything

Section titled “The line that changes everything”

Most changelog entries are incremental. Fix a bug, add a flag, shave some milliseconds. /remote-control is different. It changes the category of what Claude Code is.

A terminal tool is something you sit in front of. A tool with /remote-control is something that works alongside you. That distinction sounds small until you live it.

Think about how you actually use Claude Code. You start a task, the agent works, you monitor and steer. Sometimes a task takes ten minutes. Sometimes forty. During that time, you’re anchored to your terminal. Not because you need to type constantly, but because you need to see what’s happening.

/remote-control breaks that anchor. Start on your laptop, continue on your phone. Check progress from the couch. Approve a file change while waiting for coffee. The session is the same. Only your screen changed.

The features that make remote work

Section titled “The features that make remote work”

/remote-control by itself would be useful but disorienting. How do you know which session to reconnect to? How do you know if the agent is still working or waiting for you?

Two other additions in 2.1.79 answer those questions:

AI-generated session titles. Session tabs in VS Code now get titles based on your first message. Instead of “Session 1”, “Session 2”, you see “Fix race condition in auth middleware” and “Add pagination to search API”. When you have three sessions and you’re picking one up on your phone, labels matter.

Show turn duration. A new toggle in /config shows how long each turn took. When you check in remotely and see “Thought for 45s”, you know the agent just finished a complex reasoning step. When you see “Thought for 2s”, you know it’s waiting for you. This is information you absorbed unconsciously when watching the terminal. Now it’s explicit, designed for the glance-and-go pattern of remote monitoring.

These three features weren’t developed in isolation. They form a remote-first developer experience.

Auth gets a new path

Section titled “Auth gets a new path”

claude auth login --console authenticates against the Anthropic Console for API billing. Before this, Console users had to configure API keys manually. Now there’s a first-class login flow.

This matters for teams. If your organization manages Claude Code through the Console, onboarding a new developer just got simpler: run claude auth login --console, authenticate, done.

Performance: 18MB lighter

Section titled “Performance: 18MB lighter”

Startup memory usage dropped by ~18MB across all scenarios. For a tool that developers launch dozens of times a day, this adds up. It won’t change how Claude Code feels in any single session, but it reduces pressure on machines running multiple instances or working in memory-constrained environments.

The non-streaming API fallback also gained a 2-minute per-attempt timeout. Before this, if the streaming endpoint failed and the fallback kicked in, a stuck request could hang the session indefinitely. Now it times out and retries. Boring fix, real impact.

The bug fixes that matter

Section titled “The bug fixes that matter”

Eleven bugs fixed. Here are the ones you’d actually notice:

claude -p subprocess hanging. If you spawned Claude Code as a subprocess without explicit stdin (common in Python scripts with subprocess.run), it would hang. Fixed. This unblocks a whole class of automation workflows.

Ctrl+C in -p mode. Wasn’t working. You couldn’t interrupt a print-mode session. Fixed.

/btw returning wrong output. When you triggered /btw (a side question) during streaming, it returned the main agent’s output instead of answering your side question. Confusing. Fixed.

Voice mode on startup. Setting voiceEnabled: true in config didn’t actually activate voice mode when Claude Code launched. You had to toggle it manually. Fixed.

Enterprise rate limiting. Enterprise users couldn’t retry when hitting 429 (rate limit) errors. For teams paying for API access, being unable to retry rate limits is a significant friction point. Fixed.

Session hooks. SessionEnd hooks didn’t fire when using interactive /resume to switch sessions. If you had cleanup logic in session-end hooks, it wasn’t running during session switches. Fixed.

Permissions navigation. Left/right arrow key navigation in /permissions wasn’t working. Minor but maddening for keyboard-driven developers. Fixed.

Status line blocking. Custom status line showed nothing when workspace trust was blocking it. Now you get a visible indication instead of blank space. Fixed.

Terminal title suppression. CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_TERMINAL_TITLE wasn’t actually preventing the terminal title from being set on startup. If you had a specific tmux or terminal configuration that conflicts with title changes, this was breaking your setup silently. Fixed.

VS Code specific

Section titled “VS Code specific”

Two VS Code improvements beyond the headline features:

  1. The thinking pill now shows “Thought for Ns” instead of just “Thinking” after a response completes. Small but useful — you can see how much reasoning went into each response.

  2. Session diff button no longer missing when opening sessions from the left sidebar. If you relied on reviewing diffs from the sidebar, this was a broken workflow. Restored.

Plugin ecosystem

Section titled “Plugin ecosystem”

${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA} was introduced in 2.1.78. This release adds CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_SEED_DIR support for multiple seed directories, separated by : on Unix and ; on Windows. Plugin developers working across multiple projects can now point to multiple seed locations without juggling a single path.

Combined with the persistent state from last release, the plugin infrastructure continues to mature toward a real platform.

What this release means

Section titled “What this release means”

Strip away the individual line items and 2.1.79 tells a story about where Claude Code is heading.

The /remote-control command and its supporting features signal that Anthropic sees Claude Code as more than a terminal tool. It’s becoming an AI development companion that adapts to how developers actually work: in motion, across devices, in fragments of attention between meetings and life.

The subprocess fix and the non-streaming timeout tell a different but equally important story: Claude Code is becoming embeddable. Automation scripts, CI pipelines, custom toolchains — the rough edges that prevented reliable programmatic use are being sanded down.

And the enterprise rate-limit fix is a quiet admission that Claude Code’s user base has shifted. This isn’t just a tool for individual hackers anymore. Teams with billing accounts and compliance requirements depend on it daily.

If you use Claude Code, update. If you’ve been running it only from your desk, try /remote-control once. The experience of watching your agent work from your phone changes how you think about the tool. It stops being a place you go. It becomes something that follows you.
